A randomized trial published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2014 (Volume 100, Issue 5, Pages 1322-1328) investigated the nutritional effects of including egg yolk in the weaning diets of both breastfed and formula-fed infants. The study aimed to assess the impact of this dietary intervention on infant growth and nutritional status. 2. Another randomized controlled trial, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2002 (Volume 75, Issue 6, Pages 1084-1092), evaluated the effects of incorporating egg yolk into the weaning diets of infants. This study focused on the nutritional outcomes and potential benefits of this dietary addition. 3. A study conducted in Cambodia, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015 (Volume 101, Issue 4, Pages 742-751), examined the effects of animal-source foods and micronutrient fortification in complementary food products. The randomized trial assessed outcomes such as body composition, iron status, and linear growth in children. 4. An observational study published in Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2007 (Volume 92, Issue 10, Pages 850-854) explored the relationship between infant feeding practices during the second six months of life and iron status. The study provided insights into how feeding methods influence iron levels in infants. 5. A study published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2003 (Volume 57, Issue 4, Pages 505-513) investigated the iron status of 12-month-old infants in a population characterized by high birth weights. The research examined the effects of body size, growth, and diet on iron levels. 6. Research published in Biological Trace Element Research in 2004 (Volume 97, Issue 3, Pages 197-214) analyzed the influence of diet on the status of iron, copper, and zinc in children under 24 months of age. The study highlighted the role of dietary intake in maintaining adequate levels of these essential trace elements. 7. A randomized trial conducted in Malawi, published in the Journal of Nutrition, evaluated the developmental outcomes of providing one egg per day to children aged 6 to 15 months. The study assessed the impact of this intervention on early childhood development. 8. A randomized controlled trial in Ecuador, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, demonstrated that introducing eggs early in complementary feeding increased biomarkers related to the choline pathway and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). These findings suggest potential cognitive and developmental benefits. 9. A study published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2011 (Volume 32, Issue 3, Pages 185-191) found that meat consumption was associated with reduced stunting among toddlers in four diverse low-income settings. The research emphasized the importance of animal-source foods in preventing growth faltering. 10. A comparative study published in Archives of Biochemistry and Biophysics in 1969 (Volume 131, Issue 1, Pages 30-48) analyzed the catalytic and physical properties of lyophilized beef erythrocyte catalase and beef liver catalase components. The findings provided insights into the biochemical properties of these enzymes. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines on complementary feeding, emphasizing the importance of introducing family foods to breastfed children. These guidelines, released in 2000, provide evidence-based recommendations for optimal infant nutrition. 12. The WHO's guiding principles for complementary feeding of breastfed children, also published in 2000, outline strategies to ensure adequate nutrition during the critical weaning period. These principles aim to support healthy growth and development. 13. A systematic assessment of the risk of bias in randomized interventional studies highlights the importance of clearly defining research questions, study populations, and sample sizes. The assessment also emphasizes the need for reliable and valid measurement of exposures and outcomes to minimize bias. 14. Observational cohort and cross-sectional studies were evaluated using the NIH quality assessment tool. Key criteria included the clarity of research objectives, population definitions, participation rates, and the validity of exposure and outcome measurements. 15. The GRADE certainty tables for complementary feeding studies, particularly those involving animal-source foods, assess the relative effects of greater versus lesser frequency of consumption. These tables evaluate outcomes such as stunting, wasting, and underweight in children, with a focus on the certainty of evidence and clinical importance. 16. Studies assessing the impact of meat consumption on child growth and nutritional outcomes often report very low certainty of evidence due to limitations such as small sample sizes, observational designs, and imprecise measurements. These factors highlight the need for more robust research. 17. Research on the effects of egg consumption in children has similarly reported very low certainty of evidence. Outcomes such as stunting, wasting, and underweight were assessed, but methodological limitations reduce the reliability of these findings. 18. Studies evaluating fish consumption in children have shown mixed results, with some evidence suggesting potential benefits for growth and nutritional status. However, the certainty of evidence remains low due to methodological challenges and limited sample sizes. 19. The methodological limitations of many studies, including lack of sample size justification, high loss to follow-up, and insufficient reporting of baseline characteristics, underscore the need for improved study designs to enhance the validity of findings. 20. The WHO's systematic reviews and guidelines on complementary feeding emphasize the critical role of animal-source foods in preventing malnutrition and supporting growth in children aged 6 to 23 months. However, the evidence base requires further strengthening to inform policy and practice.
